[中文版](coming-from-stata-zh.html)

For chapter navigation, search and expandable alternatives, open the
**[Stata to R Reference](https://www.socimh.com/stata-to-r/)**.
The book has English and Chinese editions with a language switch on each chapter.
This page remains available as the single-page reference.

If you know Stata, you already know what you want to do; the question is how
to say it in R. This page lists Stata commands next to the R code that does the
same job, using tidystata where it has a Stata-style function and the standard
package everywhere else.

## Look it up from the console

`findit()` searches the same list from R. Type one Stata word bare, or quote
anything longer. Stata's abbreviations work.

```{r}
findit(reg)
findit("merge 1:1 id, keep(match)")
```

You can also look up an R function (`findit(left_join)`) or ask a question
(`findit("how do I remove duplicate rows")`). The console shows the best matches;
the returned table contains all matches. Call `findit()` for the whole list.
Descriptions follow R's language setting; English and Chinese queries both work.

Comma-separated names customize compatible examples, such as
`findit(tab, sex, region)`. The default shows one preferred answer when the task
is clear; `findit(tab) |> print(n = Inf)` shows all variants, selected alternative
R approaches, qualifications and source links. Package-qualified lookups such as
`findit(dplyr::filter)` distinguish functions with the same name.

This reference contains `r counts$commands` command families,
`r counts$functions` Stata functions and `r counts$operators` operators, with
`r counts$stata_examples` distinct Stata examples and `r counts$examples` paired
R examples. Abbreviations and alternative R implementations do not increase the
command count. The R index describes `r counts$r_functions` function/package pairs.

## Use the command tables

The tables cover tidystata and other R packages, including modelling, reshaping,
survey analysis and graphics. For panel lags and leads, tidystata provides
`stata_lag()`, `stata_lead()` and `stata_diff()`; specify the time column and
use `.by` to identify panels.

The index is alphabetical; tables are grouped by subject and sorted by command,
preferred answer and example. A package named beside a snippet is needed to run
that snippet, but `findit()` itself does not load or install reference packages.
The label names the primary package, rather than every helper dependency;
the R function index identifies additional functions and their packages.

A note that begins **Differs from Stata** means the R code does the same job,
but a default, the missing-value handling, an estimator or the output layout
differs; the note says how. Other notes are practical tips. Most R snippets are
run against controlled checks when the catalogue is built; this tests the R code
itself, not numerical agreement with Stata. Missing-value comparisons, weights, factor
reference levels, join rules and standard-error corrections need particular care.
Known gaps are explained explicitly, and related search results are not a
translation of unsupported syntax.

In the tables below, `data` is your dataset, `data1` and `data2` are the master
and using data of a merge, and `fit` is a fitted model. Most entries use dplyr,
so attach it with `library(dplyr)` or `library(tidyverse)`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, results = "asis"}
cat(tidystata:::findit_reference_html(FALSE), sep = "\n")
```
